name: Pan-Americanism
summary: Pan-Americanism is the policy of cooperation among the states of the Western Hemisphere that grew from Bolivar's call for union and Blaine's 1889 conference into the Pan-American Union and the OAS. It stresses the equality and sovereignty of states, non-intervention, no conquest, peaceful settlement of disputes, collective defence, representative democracy and, from the 1950s, cooperative economic and social development. It is a diplomatic framework, silent on most domestic questions.
scope: The inter-American system as stated in its own texts: the 1889-90 conference and Pan-American Union, the Montevideo (1933), Buenos Aires (1936) and Chapultepec (1945) declarations, the Rio Treaty, Pact of Bogota and OAS Charter, the Act of Bogota and Alliance for Progress, the 1967 presidents' declaration and the Democratic Charter, with statesmen's definitions (Blaine, Root, Lansing, Barrett, Drago) and Lockey's scholarship. It excludes Bolivarian anti-US and Marxist readings, US hegemonic readings of the Monroe Doctrine, and general liberal, democratic or development values not stated by the system.

collective-defense.rationale: Article 3 of the Rio Treaty and Article 3(h) of the OAS Charter say an armed attack on one American state is an attack on all, and the Act of Chapultepec and 1936 declaration say the same.

territorial-expansion.rationale: The movement's norms proscribe territorial conquest: the 1936 declaration, Montevideo Art. 11 and Charter Art. 3(g) say acquisitions by force give no rights and territory is inviolable.

humanitarian-intervention.rationale: Charter Art. 19 says no state or group of states may intervene, directly or indirectly, for any reason whatever, and Montevideo Art. 8 says no state has the right to intervene in the affairs of another.

national-self-determination.rationale: The system holds that each state freely chooses its own political, economic and social system (Charter Art. 3(e), Caracas, San Jose) and the Monroe Doctrine closed the hemisphere to new colonization; it speaks of states, not stateless nations.

civilizing-tutelage.rationale: Juridical equality of states, whose rights do not depend on their power (Montevideo Art. 4), plus non-intervention and the rejection of colonization, cannot be squared with one society ruling a less advanced one.

annexed-territory-occupation.rationale: Montevideo Art. 11 and the 1936 declaration bind states not to recognize territorial acquisitions obtained by force and call territory inviolable; neither speaks of the consent of the population.

end-foreign-alliances.rationale: The Rio Treaty is a standing mutual-defence alliance, central to the system, so ending permanent military alliances contradicts it.

pool-sovereignty.rationale: Barrett defines Pan-Americanism as concerted action 'without infringement' of sovereignty and the OAS Charter gives the organization only the powers it expressly confers; Latin American common-market aims are cooperation among sovereign states.

nation-first.rationale: Lansing calls Pan-Americanism internationalism, the antidote to the 'cardinal evils' of nationalism, and Root and Blaine, as quoted by Lockey, reject advancing by pulling others down; though hemispheric rather than global cooperation.

national-mission.rationale: San Jose declares that no American state may intervene to impose its ideologies or political principles on another, which rules out a mission to spread one's own form of government by pressure; a mission by example is not addressed.

independent-nuclear-deterrent.rationale: The 1967 presidents' declaration hoped for the early entry into force of the treaty banning nuclear arms in Latin America.

empower-police-military.rationale: In 1967 the presidents pledged to limit military spending to what national security actually requires and to put resources into development, and Blaine in 1889 held that standing armies beyond public order needs should be unknown.

economic-self-sufficiency.rationale: Pan-Americanism is held to be in no sense anti-European or anti-Asian (Barrett, Rio Branco), and the 1967 declaration seeks nondiscriminatory access to world markets for Latin American goods.

delink-world-market.rationale: The Alliance for Progress and the 1967 declaration seek external capital, trade access and better terms in world markets for Latin America, not a break with rich countries.

free-trade.rationale: Blaine and Clay favoured hemispheric free trade and reciprocity, while Latin American delegates in 1889 rejected a customs union and the OAS Charter seeks preferential treatment for developing countries and a Latin American common market: the strands differ.

property-fundamental.rationale: The American Declaration recognizes a right to private property tied to decent living, while the Act of Bogota and Alliance for Progress call for land-tenure reform that replaces latifundia: the record points both ways.

democracy-best.rationale: Representative democracy is the basis of political organization in the OAS Charter (Art. 3(d)), the Democratic Charter declares a right to democracy, and the Punta del Este resolution calls communism incompatible with the system; no text addresses voters choosing badly.

consent-of-governed.rationale: The OAS Charter and Democratic Charter rest legitimate rule on representative democracy and free and fair elections, and bar governments installed by unconstitutional interruption.

separated-powers.rationale: The Democratic Charter lists separation of powers and independence of branches among the essential elements of representative democracy (Art. 3).

courts-bound-by-majority.rationale: Separation of powers, the rule of law and independent branches are essential elements of democracy in the Democratic Charter, so courts that may not constrain a majority conflict with it.

sovereign-above-law.rationale: Access to and exercise of power must be subject to the rule of law and state institutions subordinate to the lawful civilian authority (Democratic Charter Art. 3-4).

one-party-rule.rationale: The 1962 Punta del Este resolution condemns the 'dictatorship of a single party' as incompatible with the inter-American system, and the Democratic Charter requires a pluralistic system of parties.

total-state.rationale: San Jose states that the inter-American system is incompatible with any form of totalitarianism.

dictatorship-of-proletariat.rationale: The 1962 resolution declares the principles of communism incompatible with the inter-American system and condemns single-party dictatorship; the Democratic Charter requires elections and pluralism.

party-controls-media.rationale: The Democratic Charter treats freedom of expression and of the press as essential to democracy (Art. 4) and the American Declaration protects freedom of expression.

party-commands-army.rationale: The Democratic Charter requires the constitutional subordination of all state institutions, armed forces included, to the legally constituted civilian authority, which a party command contradicts.

censor-art-for-virtue.rationale: The American Declaration protects freedom of investigation, opinion, expression and dissemination, which censoring art for its moral effect contradicts.

equal-moral-worth.rationale: The American Declaration (Art. II) guarantees equality before the law regardless of race, sex, language or creed and Charter Art. 3(l) proclaims fundamental rights without discrimination.

racial-segregation-law.rationale: Charter Art. 3(l) and American Declaration Art. II rule out discrimination by race, and the 1967 presidents resolved that racial equality must be effective.

distinct-gender-roles.rationale: Charter Art. 3(l) and the American Declaration guarantee rights without discrimination by sex and the Democratic Charter calls for women's full and equal participation in politics.

conscription.rationale: Only a generic duty clause of the 1948 American Declaration of the Rights and Duties of Man (military service, paying taxes), not a position of Pan-Americanism as a doctrine.

taxation-theft.rationale: Only a generic duty clause of the 1948 American Declaration of the Rights and Duties of Man (military service, paying taxes), not a position of Pan-Americanism as a doctrine.

unions-good.rationale: The OAS Charter (Art. 45) recognizes workers' rights to organize, bargain collectively and strike, and the contribution of labor unions to the life of society and to development.

class-collaboration.rationale: The Alliance for Progress calls for procedures of consultation and collaboration among public authorities, employer associations and labor organizations.

tax-the-wealthy.rationale: The Alliance for Progress charter calls for tax reform including fair and adequate taxation of large incomes and real estate.

land-redistribution.rationale: The Alliance for Progress calls for agrarian reform replacing latifundia and dwarf holdings with an equitable system of land tenure so the land becomes the basis of the man who works it, country by country, while the Act of Bogota speaks of examining land tenure for wider ownership.

priority-to-poor.rationale: The Alliance for Progress sets as goals raising the income of the needier sectors fastest and projects that meet the most pressing social needs, and the Charter makes eliminating extreme poverty a shared responsibility.

cut-welfare.rationale: The Charter (Art. 45) and the American Declaration (Art. XVI) call for social security policies for the old, the unemployed and the disabled.

ban-cartels.rationale: The Alliance for Progress calls for more competitive markets and for preventing monopolistic practices.

population-causes-poverty.rationale: The Act of Bogota and the Alliance for Progress trace social ills to institutions such as unjust land tenure and call for institutional reform alongside growth.

restrict-freedoms-for-growth.rationale: The Alliance for Progress pursues development 'in accordance with democratic principles' and a 'free, just and democratic order' (1967) rather than a trade of freedoms for growth.

competition-drives-progress.rationale: The movement's statesmen (Lansing, Root, Blaine, Drago, as quoted by Lockey) frame it as cooperation and 'no victories but those of peace', rejecting profit from pulling others down.
